subject: [PATCH v5 0/7] move stock from mem_cgroup to page_counter

reviews.author: Michal Koutný
reviews.summary:
Reviewer noted that the patch does not handle the case where a page_counter is being drained while its stock is still in use, and requested the addition of a check to ensure that the stock is dropped before draining.

Reviewer noted that page_counter_drain_stock_async() may have performance implications and suggested guarding v1 code in drain_all_stock() with !cgroup_on_dfl(memcg->css.cgroup) to mitigate potential issues.
reviews.raw_body:
Hello Joshua.

On Mon, Aug 31, 2026 at 09:37:51AM -0700, Joshua Hahn <joshua.hahnjy@gmail.com> wrote:

---

(Just a passerby comment, I have no remarks to the overhaul.)

The change of do_memsw_account() is because of re-attaching the memory
controller between v1 and v2 trees. That's not so common operation (but
not ruled out), pre-condition for that is that there's only a single
online memcg, namely the root memcg. So it needs treatment especially at
memcg offlining (which is what drain_all_stock() (also) does).

I don't know how expensive page_counter_drain_stock_async() is going to
be [1] but the v1 parts here could could be guarded with
!cgroup_on_dfl(memcg->css.cgroup).

Regards,
Michal

[1] Now, I see in 5/7 that there's the counter->stock check which should
    be quick bailout on v2 (maybe quicker than the cgroup_on_dfl()
    Iproposed above).

reviews.author: Joshua Hahn (author)
reviews.summary:
Author acknowledged lack of experience with cgroup v1 and recognized the need for guarding, but did not indicate a plan to address this issue in the patch.

Author responded to concerns about performance impact of draining stock, explaining that the function itself is quick and only schedules a job item.

Author responded to reviewer's unclear question about why cgroup_on_dfl() is not present in the code, stating that it should achieve the same goal and was likely omitted for simplicity.
reviews.raw_body:
Wow, that's good to know. To be completely honest I dont have much
experience with cgroup v1. I didn't realize it wasn't a "switch whenever
you want" type of operation. Good to know that there is some more
guarding there.

---

The function itself should be pretty quick. It just frees one CPU's
stock, but the rest is just scheduling a job item.

---

I'm not entirely sure, it's probably similar : -)
I think they should achieve the same goal, and hopefully it wasn't too
difficult to understand why we don't have the cgroup_on_dfl() there.

Hopefully the rest of the code looks good to you too. Thanks again for
taking a look Michal, I hope you have a great day!
Joshua

2026-09-01.patch_summary: This patch series moves the per-cpu 'stock' from mem_cgroup to page_counter, allowing for more efficient and independent stock management. The stock is now a property of each counter rather than the CPU, eliminating the need for cross-memcg interference and random victim eviction. This change also enables transparent charging and refilling of stock through page_counter_try_charge(). As a result, multiple sources of stock management can be added to mem_cgroup without tightly coupling them to struct mem_cgroup.

reviews.author: Joshua Hahn (author)
reviews.summary: Author responded to a concern about Sashiko's review, stating that they had no concerns with the series and thanking reviewers for their feedback.

reviews.author: Shakeel Butt
reviews.summary: Reviewer Shakeel Butt reported a compilation error on GCC 14.2.1 due to missing include directive for the page_counter_stock struct, which is declared as __percpu, requiring an appropriate header to be included.
reviews.raw_body:
On gcc 14.2.1, I get

In file included from mm/page_counter.c:8:
./include/linux/page_counter.h:47:44: error: expected \u2018:\u2019, \u2018,\u2019, \u2018;\u2019, \u2018}\u2019 or \u2018__attribute__\u2019 before \u2018*\u2019 token
   47 |         struct page_counter_stock __percpu *stock;
      |                                            ^

I think you need an appropriate header in this file.

reviews.author: Shakeel Butt
reviews.summary: Reviewer Shakeel Butt pointed out that the patch description uses confusing terminology, specifically 'growing the hierarchy size' and 'hierarchy size growth', which should be clarified.
reviews.raw_body:
The terminology of "growing the hierarchy size" and "hierarchy size growth" is
confusing.

The code looks fine.

reviews.author: Shakeel Butt
reviews.summary: Reviewer Shakeel Butt requested adding a gfp parameter to the function and suggested using it instead of hardcoding __GFP_ACCOUNT, also recommending the use of set_active_memcg() at the caller to charge the parent memcg instead of the one creating the memcg.
reviews.raw_body:
Let's add gfp param to the function and use that here. Also if you want to use
__GFP_ACCOUNT then you should use set_active_memcg() at the caller, so you don't
charge the one creating the memcg but the parent similar to what
mem_cgroup_css_alloc() does.

reviews.author: Shakeel Butt
reviews.summary:
Reviewer Shakeel Butt expressed confusion about the handling of nested NMI in the patch, specifically mentioning that it is unclear what this comment is trying to say and finding the explanation confusing.

Reviewer Shakeel Butt noted that the patch disables stocks for memcg charges in NMI context, and questioned why this is done, suggesting it may be due to a misunderstanding of spin_lock behavior on UP systems.

Reviewer Shakeel Butt expressed concerns about the introduction of atomic operations and IRQ toggling on the fast path, questioning their necessity and suggesting a decoupling of design decisions to first move stock to page counter without spin locks or remote draining, then convert later in the series with performance numbers.
reviews.raw_body:
I don't understand what this comment is trying to say. The nested NMI is
confusing.

---

You are completely disabling stocks for memcg charges in nmi context. Why? I
assume that is what the comment above trying to explain but it is failing.

IIUC you want to use spin_lock instead of local_trylock because you want to
support draining from remote cpus and spin_lock on UP are simply disable irq and
does not protect from NMI. Maybe you need spin_trylock similar to local_trylock.
Not saying you to implement that but please explain stuff clearly.

---

Why do you need to disable irqs?

Anyways, you are changing the fast path of the charge drastically. Previously
there was no atomic ops and not irq toggling but this patch is adding atomic op
and irq toggle (not sure about why irq toggle is needed) on the fast path.

I understand that remote draining is the only reason you need to use spin locks
here otherwise you will need to allocate work_struct in page_counter_stock. You
are making these design decisions very silently and implicitly.

How about we decouple the decision of remote drain / spin lock from moving stock
inside page counter? First move the stock to page counter without any spin lock
or remote drain and later in the series you convert to spin lock plus remote
draining with performance numbers.

reviews.author: Shakeel Butt
reviews.summary: Reviewer Shakeel Butt questioned the necessity of asynchronous draining, suggesting that synchronous draining should be used instead.
reviews.raw_body:
But you are introducing remote draining. Why do you need async drainer at all?
Just always drain synchronously.

reviews.author: Joshua Hahn (author)
reviews.summary:
Author acknowledged a concern about the stock refill path and agreed to restructure it in v2, but did not provide a specific fix or timeline.

Author acknowledged that the patch series is complicated due to trying to do two things at once, agreed to split it into two separate patches: one for migrating to page_counter and another for addressing the drainers.
reviews.raw_body:
On Mon, 7 Sep 2026 16:25:31 -0700 Shakeel Butt <shakeel.butt@linux.dev> wrote:

Hi Shakeel,

Thanks for your review on the series!

---

I was trying to match parity with the existing code as much as possible.
But I see now that this series is a bit complicated because I'm trying
to do two things at once and mixing up the page_counter migration
and the scalable draining together.

In the next version I'll keep parity and only migrate to page_counter
and in a follow-up I'll address the drainers separately.

Thanks again!
Joshua

reviews.author: Joshua Hahn (author)
reviews.summary:
Author acknowledged a concern about nested NMI and ordering protection for stock access, promised to clarify and address it in the next version.

Author acknowledged that their previous explanation was unclear and promised to restructure the code in the next version.

Author acknowledged reviewer feedback about draining an exact CPU, agreeing that fungibility is sufficient and promising to rework the explanation in a future version.

Author agreed to restructure the patch in v2 to address reviewer's feedback about the swapoff path needing to drop the per-vswap spinlock before calling try_to_unmap().
reviews.raw_body:
Hi Shakeel, thanks for your review on the series!

Yes, I'm sorry about that. There were a few layers of protection that
I wanted to make against nested NMI, ordering, publishing for stock, 
etc. I think I didn't make it clear what was happening, so I'll
address that in the next version.

---

Yes, that's exactly what it is. I think there was a lot of thinking
on my end on things to look out for that in the end it just kind of
became a jumbled mess, I'll definitely do a re-spin of what's happening
in the next version.

---

All I was trying to say here is that we don't need to drain an exact
CPU, all we need to do is to try and get any CPU. So if we migrate
and get a different CPU's ptr than we initially started with, it's no
big deal (that's what I tried to explain with saying that stock is
fungible). But I agree it's a little lacking in explanation here,
I'll rework it in the next version.

---

That sounds like a good plan to me. I'll do exactly that and send a
new version.

Thank you for your time Shakeel, I hope you have a great rest of your
day! : -)
Joshua
